paras: The lynching of Sidney King was the hanging of a Black man in Hernando County, Florida, after he was accused of shooting and cutting the three children of Sheriff J. B. Mickler on June 29, 1881. According to a Jacksonville dispatch, King was captured, confessed, and was hanged in the presence and with the approval of two hundred citizens. The dispatch ran in papers from Georgia to Wisconsin, and the Savannah Morning News, while condemning mob law, called the execution 'little wonder'.

Mickler was sheriff of Hernando County and, according to the Jacksonville dispatch, lived some miles from the courthouse. The Weekly Floridian, relying on Captain Burroughs, the state timber agent, added that the sheriff had lost his wife about three weeks earlier. The wire called the accused only 'a negro named King', while the Savannah Morning News named him Sidney King, seventeen, whom the sheriff had 'rescued from the clutches of the law'.

On June 29, the dispatch said, Mickler went to the courthouse and left his three children, aged eight, eleven and fourteen, alone with King. King was accused of shooting and mortally wounding the oldest, driving the other two into the woods, shooting the elder of them dead and cutting the throat of the younger, who was left for dead. He was then said to have robbed the house and lain in wait to kill the sheriff, but neighbors returned with Mickler and the attempt failed. A Floridian informant said instead that the oldest child was about eight and that the man, discovered by the children in a theft, shot two and cut the throat of the third.

The wounded children were able to say what had happened, and King was captured and, by the wire's account, confessed. He was hanged before a crowd the dispatch put at two hundred citizens and 'died sullen and unrepenting'; a shorter version in the Daily Kennebec Journal said he was hung by 'an angered mob'. The Savannah editorial wrote that 'a whole community rose up as one man, pursued, captured and promptly executed' him, and a Kentucky brief said he was arrested before he was lynched. None of the reports gives the date or place of the hanging, the names of those who carried it out, or whether any officer was present.

No report of an inquest, arrest or official inquiry into the hanging appears in the coverage. First reports said 'one and perhaps both' of the wounded children were dead, and Wisconsin papers later called them critical. On July 26 the Weekly Floridian reported that the youngest, Bloxham, was recovering from the knife wounds inflicted by 'the murderer Sidney King'.

The Jacksonville dispatch of July 5 appeared the next day in the Savannah Morning News under the headlines 'The Fate of a Fiend' and 'The Miscreant Promptly Lynched', and on the same day in New York, Lancaster, Wheeling, Chicago, Memphis, Washington and Dallas. Headline writers called it 'Swift Justice' and 'Quick Justice', and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer presented King as 'A Black Piend [Fiend]' who 'Murders in Cold Blood the Children of His Benefactor'. Northern reprints added that the crowd was 'white and colored', and the Chicago Tribune printed its size as 20 rather than 200.

Condensed items followed in weeklies through mid-July, among them the South Kentuckian, which called King an 'ungrateful wretch', and Wisconsin papers that spelled the sheriff's name Micken or Mackler and placed Hernando County in Mississippi. The Savannah Morning News alone commented editorially, calling the killings the climax of 'cold-blooded, fiendish outrage' and saying that mob law was 'to be condemned in the strongest terms' while finding the execution unsurprising. In Florida the Weekly Floridian handled the case as state news gathered second-hand from a timber agent and 'the Union of Sunday', and later reported on the surviving child.

Accounts differed on the children: the wire gave their ages as eight, eleven and fourteen and the Floridian's informant put the oldest at about eight. Although headlines spoke of a 'triple murder' and several briefs said all three children were murdered, the wire's own text reported one child killed outright, and the later Floridian report shows the youngest survived.

reader.title: Lynching of Sidney King
bases: A Black man accused of shooting and cutting a sheriff's children was captured and hanged by citizens without trial (A2, A3, A17).

King was hanged after capture with no legal proceeding, before and with the approval of a crowd reported as two hundred citizens (A2); the Savannah Morning News called it 'mob law' carried out by the community, and the Floridian and Kennebec Journal said he was 'lynched' or hung by 'an angered mob' (A3, A17, A1).

The Jacksonville wire (A2), the Floridian's report drawn from the Union (A16, A17) and the Savannah editorial with its own details (A3) agree that the accused was captured and lynched, though the two Florida-sourced reports may share an origin.

framing.detail: The wire called King a 'fiend' and 'miscreant' and stressed the crowd's 'approbation'; Savannah's headline was 'The Miscreant Promptly Lynched'.
The Savannah editorial said mob law 'is to be condemned in the strongest terms' yet found it 'little wonder' the community executed him.
Northern and Western dailies ran the wire under 'Swift Justice', 'Quick Justice', 'A Black Fiend' and 'Triple Murder and Lynching'.
The Weekly Floridian reported the case as state news from local informants and followed the surviving child's recovery.
